title: 12 Months of Unity Dev with Claude Code
summary: A 3D artist building a Unity game with Claude Code argues AI pulls code toward average quality, which helps novices far more than strong engineers, and shows his planning workflow.

assertions.quote: Claude code is always pulling everything towards the average.

verdicts.note: Several studies find reduced diversity of ideas and phrasing with LLM assistance (creative writing, ideation); consistent with the MIT result.

assertions.quote: So in my case if I'm starting at almost near zero and it bumps me into average code the multiplier is insane.

verdicts.note: Experts get more reliable results and catch errors, but several RCTs show larger measured speedups for juniors, and METR found experts slowed; contested.

assertions.quote: eventually, it will just be very average. That is not a fun workflow.

verdicts.note: Consistent with long-horizon benchmarks such as SlopCodeBench and with studies of AI-code churn and duplication. Evidence is early but points the same way.

assertions.quote: I am an artist and I'm using cloud code to do stuff that traditionally an artist wouldn't jump into

verdicts.note: Tools like Lovable, v0, Replit let non-developers produce working prototypes; widely observed.

assertions.quote: it asks Claude to only ask me one question at a time, wait for me to respond

verdicts.note: Requirements clarification before implementation is well-established practice and widely reported to reduce agent rework.

assertions.quote: It just helps Claude pause at the end and give me an implementation plan just get final approval on

verdicts.note: Plan-then-execute consistently reduces agent rework in practice and in vendor evals, especially on multi-file tasks.

assertions.quote: Throwaway tools. It doesn't really matter if it's average, below average, whatever.

verdicts.note: Direction is well supported: greenfield, low-stakes work gets the biggest gains in studies and surveys. The specific multipliers are anecdote.
